title: ECG foundation models for cardiovascular screening in a cohort of young competitive athletes
desc: AI-powered cardiac screening could evolve sports medicine by boosting accuracy, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness, with automated ECG interpretation based on foundation models becoming key for large-scale athlete screening. Before deployment, it is crucial to verify whether these clinically developed models are applicable to this population. We evaluated whether ECG foundation models trained on general clinical populations can diagnose athlete-specific ECG findings. We fine-tuned three models (ECG-FM, HuBERT-ECG, ECGFounder) on PhysioNet/CinC 2021, 87,662 samples, and tested them on 43 expert-annotated ECGs from highly trained/national-level athletes. Performance was strong on PhysioNet/CinC 2021 (AUROC 0.97, AUPRC 0.57, Sensitivity 0.89) but dropped on athletes’ data, confirming domain shift. ECGFounder performed best (AUROC 0.84, AUPRC 0.72, Sensitivity 0.57) and detected the most frequent findings, Sinus Bradycardia (AUROC 0.87) and Sinus Arrhythmia (AUROC 0.95), well. Per-label estimates for rare classes must be interpreted cautiously, given the small cohort. This work contributes to developing athlete-focused AI frameworks for reliable ECG-based screening.

title: Generative AI adoption is more widespread than predictive AI at US hospitals.
desc: [Health affairs scholar] Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among U.S. hospitals has accelerated rapidly, yet national estimates of predictive and generative AI implementation across clinical and administrative settings remain limited. Using data from 2203 nonfederal acute care hospitals in the 2025 American Hospital Association Information Technology Survey, we described AI adoption, model source (electronic health record [EHR] developer, third-party developer, or self-developed), and specific clinical and administrative use cases. We assessed associations between hospital and area characteristics and AI adoption, model source, and number of AI use cases using weighted multivariable regression. In 2025, 81% of hospitals reported using AI, with 77% of hospitals using generative AI-more than double the rate reported in 2024. The most common applications were ambient documentation (73%) and predicting health trajectories or risks (70%). System affiliation and use of the market-leading EHR were the strongest predictors of AI adoption. Hospitals using EHR-developed AI reported 2.48 additional AI use cases (95% CI, 1.93-3.03). Generative AI adoption surpassed predictive AI for the first time, driven by ambient documentation. While use of EHR-developed AI was associated with greater use, there was a greater influence of third-party vendors for generative AI compared to predictive AI. Continued monitoring will be essential to assess AI's impact across healthcare.

AI-driven Immuno-Radio-Multi-Omics in triple-negative breast cancer: mapping the immune landscape for precision immunotherapy.
desc: [Frontiers in immunology] In triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) is highly heterogeneous and constitutes a key determinant of response to immunotherapy. Nevertheless, current clinical assessment of biomarkers, notably programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), relies primarily on static and localized tissue sampling, constrained by spatial heterogeneity, sampling bias, and lack of longitudinal assessment, which limits its capacity to fully represent the evolving TIME and support adaptive treatment decision-making. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven radiomics has emerged as a non-invasive framework enabling the conversion of routine imaging into high-throughput biomarkers, capturing TIME imaging phenotypes. When integrated with genomic data, this strategy extends into radiogenomics, allowing the association of radiomics features with underlying molecular features to better characterize the TNBC landscape. However, given the inter/intra-diversity of TNBC-TIME, integrating complementary multi-omics layers becomes necessary to fully reflect TIME landscape and represent the interplay between TIME components. Several findings from studies on solid tumors, including TNBC, suggest that AI-derived radiomics signatures are associated with immune and molecular patterns and may predict PD-L1 expression, TILs, TIME phenotypes and response to immune checkpoint blockade. Beyond static and isolated biomarker development, 'Immuno-Radio-Multi-Omics' could enable dynamic non-invasive whole-tumor immune profiling, enhanced patient stratification, and support the future development of longitudinal and adaptive therapeutic strategies. Meanwhile, its clinical translation is currently limited by the lack of large and prospective datasets, standardization, validation and interpretability. Through this mini-review, we aim to critically discuss current evidence, limitations and next frontiers of 'Immuno-Radio-Multi-Omics' in TNBC, emphasizing its potential to advance dynamic and personalized immunotherapy strategies in TNBC.

The Transformative Role of Artificial Intelligence in Wearable Health Monitoring: Applications in Diagnosis, Therapy, and Rehabilitation.
source: PubMed · Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
desc: [Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)] This chapter explores the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented wearable technology in dynamic health monitoring across diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation. Innovations include real-time cardiovascular disease detection, AI-driven continuous glucose monitoring for diabetes, and neurological disorder tracking using flexible electroencephalograph (EEG) sensors. Therapeutic advances feature smart drug-delivery patches responsive to biomarkers, remote intervention systems, and surgical tools like augmented reality (AR) navigation. Rehabilitation breakthroughs encompass wearables for motor recovery, cardiopulmonary optimization, and neurorehabilitation using brain-computer interfaces. Future progress hinges on multifunctional hardware, federated learning for privacy, explainable AI, and standardized regulations.

Artificial Intelligence in Precision Nutrition: From Multi-Omics Integration to Personalized Dietary Interventions.
desc: [Clinical nutrition ESPEN] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated as a tool for precision nutrition because it can analyse heterogeneous dietary, clinical, physiological, behavioural, and molecular data. This narrative review critically examines how machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, explainable AI, continuous glucose monitoring, wearable technologies, and multi-omics approaches may support individualized nutritional assessment and decision-making. Particular attention is given to the distinction between predictive research, digital personalized nutrition, AI-enabled clinical interventions, and commercial nutrition platforms. Current evidence shows that personalized digital nutrition can improve selected dietary behaviours, while observational AI and multi-omics studies can predict substantial inter-individual variation in metabolic responses. Importantly, evidence that an AI-enabled intervention improves clinical outcomes is still limited and is concentrated in selected settings, including a multicentre randomized trial of an AI-based dietary management platform in adults with type 2 diabetes. Emerging technologies such as large language models, digital twins, federated learning, and adaptive algorithms remain promising but require prospective clinical validation. Major barriers include data quality, algorithmic bias, privacy, interoperability, model transparency, regulatory uncertainty, and limited external validation. Future research should prioritize pragmatic multicentre randomized trials, transparent reporting of model performance, independent validation, health-economic evaluation, and clinically meaningful outcomes. AI should therefore be considered an adjunct to evidence-based nutritional care rather than a replacement for professional clinical judgement. The review differs from technology-centred and methodology-focused reviews by explicitly linking AI modalities and multi-omics data with evidence maturity, clinical trial findings, implementation barriers, and the level of inference justified for each technology.

Potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence to address disparities in epilepsy.
desc: [Nature reviews. Neurology] The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and health care offers unprecedented opportunities to address global disparities in access to specialized epilepsy diagnosis and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advances in AI models, combined with increasing internet connectivity and smartphone usage in low-income and middle-income countries, offer promising solutions for epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring through AI-based analysis of electroencephalography recordings captured with affordable open-source systems, smartphone data and electronic health records. However, this technological revolution raises important questions about the preservation and expansion of clinical expertise, AI algorithm transparency and health-care equity. In this Review, we examine how AI can help to address disparities and improve global epilepsy care while maintaining high clinical standards and addressing systemic challenges.

Calibrating trust in generative artificial intelligence for clinical communication through Chinese medical humanism.
desc: [Frontiers in public health] Generative artificial intelligence is entering clinical communication through patient messaging, health education, and conversational decision support. Its capacity to produce reassuring language can coexist with inaccurate advice, unclear responsibility, and culturally inappropriate explanations. This mini-review examines how Chinese medical humanism can inform the calibration of trust in these encounters. Targeted literature identification integrates studies of trust and perceived empathy, research on traditional Chinese medicine communication, and medical education evidence with normative scholarship. The evidence distinguishes perceived empathy from relational accountability and technical performance from demonstrated patient benefit. Chinese medical ideals of benevolence, sincerity, holistic attention, and contextual judgment offer resources for interpreting professional responsibilities, but their incorporation into artificial intelligence has not been shown to restore trust or improve health outcomes. We synthesize these insights into a proposed dual-verification approach: an epistemic track checks evidence, uncertainty, and safety, while a relational track checks patient understanding, cultural meaning, preferences, and access to human care. Their convergence supports accountable communication and allows unresolved concerns to trigger human review. Educational applications connect critical appraisal of generated responses with reflection on classical medical ethics. Evaluation should prioritize appropriate reliance, error recognition, patient agency, and equitable access rather than maximizing trust scores. This approach reframes humanistic integration as a set of responsibilities for clinicians and institutions, with its effectiveness remaining an empirical question.

Individual Probability of Successful Extubation Using a Neural Network: A Proof-of-Concept Analysis.
desc: [Rhode Island medical journal (2013)] Studies have shown that artificial intelligence can aid in extubating patients from ventilators, but none have used predominantly respiratory parameters to yield a simple probability of successful extubation that can immediately aid clinicians in their decision to extubate or not extubate patients. We sought to determine whether it is possible to create a neural network as a proof-of-concept analysis using predominantly respiratory parameters to derive a single probability of successful extubation for an individual patient. Fourteen predominantly respiratory parameters were the input for a neural network with one hidden layer to yield a single output, a simple probability of extubation. The system trained on 17 patients, 13 of whom successfully extubated, four of whom failed. The results showed excellent separation between the extubation successes and failures. When applied to the test group of four patients, there also was excellent separation between the three successful extubations (prediction range: 98.8% to 100% probability) and the one failure (2.9% probability). This proof-of-concept analysis showed that it is possible to use predominantly respiratory parameters to present a single number, a probability of extubation, as the output from a neural network. This analysis needs to be performed on a larger sample before it can be applied confidently, but the framework now is available for further development to assist intensivists who work with ventilated patients.

Deep learning reconstruction for low-dose thoracic CT of calcification inserts: A phantom study of CNR, noise magnitude, and noise texture.
source: PubMed · Journal of applied clinical medical physics
desc: [Journal of applied clinical medical physics] To compare filtered back projection (FBP), 50% Adaptive Statistical Iterative Reconstruction-Veo (ASiR), and medium-strength deep learning image reconstruction (DLIR) for hydroxyapatite calcification inserts under different dose, tube-voltage, and phantom-size conditions using contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), background noise magnitude, and noise power spectrum (NPS) analysis. A QRM-Thorax containing a QRM-CCI D100 cardiac calcification insert was scanned on a GE Revolution Apex CT system using institution-defined routine and low-dose protocols at 80, 100, 120, and 140 kVp, with and without an Extension Ring L. Images were reconstructed at 2.5-mm thickness using FBP, ASiR, and DLIR. CNR was evaluated for 3- and 5-mm inserts at 200, 400, and 800 mg HA/cm3. Background noise was assessed from a calcification-excluded mask. For NPS analysis, 10 calcification-free images were analyzed for each acquisition condition. Total two-dimensional NPS power, power-weighted normalized radial NPS, and power-weighted mean spatial frequency were calculated. DLIR reduced background noise magnitude and increased CNR relative to FBP across the evaluated conditions, whereas differences relative to ASiR varied with insert size, density, tube voltage, and phantom size. Across all 16 protocol, phantom-size, and tube-voltage combinations, ASiR and DLIR reduced total 2D NPS power by 58.1% and 75.8%, respectively, relative to FBP; DLIR reduced total power by 41.9% relative to ASiR. ASiR produced a more consistent shift toward lower power-weighted mean spatial frequencies, averaging 12.4% below FBP, whereas the shift with DLIR was smaller and more condition dependent, averaging 3.2% below FBP. In this controlled phantom study, DLIR reduced total noise power and improved CNR relative to FBP, but its incremental difference from ASiR was task and protocol dependent. CNR and noise magnitude should be interpreted together with NPS because nonlinear reconstruction methods can alter both noise magnitude and spatial-frequency distribution.

title: Evaluating readability of AI-generated pediatric dental education materials.
desc: [Frontiers in digital health] General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have become a popular source of oral health information. However, the patient education materials (PEMs) generated by these models often pose readability challenges. This study aimed to: (1) compare the readability of PEMs generated by six AI chatbots in response to ten frequently asked questions on pediatric oral health; and (2) determine whether the readability of these texts meets the level recommended by the American Medical Association (AMA). Ten sample questions on pediatric oral health were compiled. Each question was submitted once to each of six AI chatbots (GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2.5, and Qwen3-Max), generating a corpus of 60 texts in a blocked (repeated-measures) design. Six readability indices - Flesch Reading Ease (FRE), Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Gunning Fog Index (GFI), Coleman-Liau Index (CLI), Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG), and Automated Readability Index (ARI) - were calculated for every text. Each index was analysed separately using the Friedman test, with the ten questions as blocks and the six models as conditions, followed by Dunn's multiple comparison test. Kendall's coefficient of concordance (W) was calculated to quantify the consistency of model ranking across questions. DeepSeek-V3 showed the highest readability (easiest texts) and Gemini 3 Flash the second highest, whereas Claude Haiku 4.5 showed the lowest readability across all six indices; GPT-5 Mini, Qwen3-Max, and Kimi K2.5 occupied intermediate positions. All six Friedman tests were statistically significant (χ 2(5) = 31.77-35.94, all p < 0.0001), and Kendall's W ranged from 0.635 to 0.719, indicating that the relative ranking of the six models was broadly consistent across the ten questions. Against the AMA-recommended sixth-grade reading level, all models exceeded the recommended difficulty on every index; even against a more lenient seventh-grade threshold, only the ARI median of DeepSeek-V3 (6.5) fell below 7. The PEMs generated by the six LLMs were written at a reading level above the AMA recommendation, and reading difficulty differed systematically among models. Readability should be explicitly controlled through prompt design, model optimisation, and professional review before such materials are used in pediatric oral health education.

title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps.
source: PubMed · bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
desc: [bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology] Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool-using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.
